### C-R5-01
- **Claim:** Goldingay frames Part 2c (14:1–17:27) as beginning by questioning Judah’s assumptions about **prayer**, after parts 1, 2a, and 2b questioned assumptions about the exodus, the temple, and Sinai; the curator’s introduction “What came as Yahweh’s message to Jeremiah” opens a further sequence after 13:23–27’s plausible ending.
- **Quote:** “As parts 1, 2a, and 2b began by questioning Judah’s assumptions about the exodus, the temple, and Sinai, part 2c begins by questioning its assumptions about prayer. After 13:23–27 made a plausible ending for one sequence of Jeremiah’s messages, the phrase What came as Yahweh’s message to Jeremiah comprises a curator’s introduction to a further sequence.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 1–6; Part 2c intro
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R5-02
- **Claim:** Goldingay outlines 14:1–15:21 as **four exchanges** of protests and responses among Yahweh, Jeremiah, and Judah; then 16:1–17:11 confrontations/warnings about country and domain; 17:12–27 another exchange with three ironies.
- **Quote:** “14:1–15:21 Four more sets of protests and responses between Yahweh, Jeremiah, and Judah … 16:1–17:11 A series of confrontations and warnings about this country and domain … 17:12–27 Another exchange between Judah, Jeremiah, and Yahweh with three ironies.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 8–22; structure of 2c
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R5-03
- **Claim:** On 14:1–12, Goldingay reads the drought poem + plea as the form of a **liturgy** (fast/famine), which Yahweh’s response turns into a “**counter-liturgy**”: people may think prayer makes a difference; Yahweh says “Not necessarily.”
- **Quote:** “The section thus begins by hinting at the form of a liturgy of the kind that people might have used during a fast … or in the context of famine…. But Yahweh’s response turns it upside down. It becomes a kind of ‘counter-liturgy.’ … They may think that prayer makes a difference. Yahweh says, ‘Not necessarily.’”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 252–253; on 14:1–12
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R5-04
- **Claim:** Goldingay holds that the rare plural **“dearths”** (*baṣṣārôt*) covers not only the drought of 14:2–9 but other deprivations in Jer 14–17; the section’s “lack of an external referent” means its teaching applies on other occasions of drought, attack, or epidemic—and prayer about them.
- **Quote:** “The rare word dearths covers the drought that is the subject of 14:2–9 but also the other deprivations that Jer 14–17 refers to; the word recurs in 17:8…. Its comment about understanding dearths and dealing with them relates not just to one situation. It needs taking into account on other occasions when the people of God experience drought, attack, or epidemic—and pray about it.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 280; on 14:1
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R5-05
- **Claim:** In Goldingay’s reading of 14:2–6, the drought poem moves from human mourning (gates, darkness, Jerusalem’s grief-shout) through empty cisterns/ditches and farmhands’ shame to animals: the hind abandons offspring for lack of grass; wild donkeys pant for rain; “no water … no rain … no grass … no vegetation.”
- **Quote:** “There is no water (v. 3) because there is no rain (v. 4) and therefore no grass (v. 5) and no vegetation (v. 6).”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 282–289; on 14:2–6
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R5-06
- **Claim:** Goldingay treats 14:7–9 as a prayer **Jeremiah devises** for Judah (Jeremiah language: “turnings”; “we have done wrong”), not a genuine popular confession; the confession deconstructs protest-psalm logic by admitting calamity is appropriate—and Yahweh sees through the prayer (14:10: “this people… like to drift”).
- **Quote:** “It is a concrete indication that the prayer is one Jeremiah is devising for them rather than one of theirs that he is quoting…. If vv. 2–6 are a quasi-protest psalm, then v. 7 deconstructs its logic…. How could Yahweh resist such a prayer…? ‘God’s response introduced by the messenger formula does not correspond to expectations’: instead of a declaration of forgiveness there is a declaration of judgment.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 290–296; on 14:7–10
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R5-07
- **Claim:** Goldingay stresses Yahweh’s unique refusal: he “does not accept them—the people themselves” (only clear example of Yahweh saying he does not accept his people); he forbids Jeremiah to plead “for good things” (14:11); fasting, whole offering, and grain offering count for nothing without change of life; **sword, hunger, and epidemic** form the “unholy trinity” of war-killers (14:12).
- **Quote:** “It is the only clear example of Yahweh ever saying he does not accept his people…. Far from accepting them, therefore, Yahweh has a threat in mind…. To sword and hunger (see 5:12) he now adds epidemic; this unholy trinity will recur…. They are the three great killers in war…. Yahweh declares the intention to do so by means of them … though of course he actually will not, even though the people do not turn.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 296–301; on 14:10–12
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R5-08
- **Claim:** On 14:13–18, Goldingay reads Jeremiah’s protest about prophets promising *šәlôm ʾĕmet* (“things being truly well”) as conflict over **shalom theology**; Yahweh calls their message deceit/false vision/empty divination/mind-originated duplicity; those prophets will perish by sword and hunger, and the people they deceive will share the fate; 14:17–18 commissions tears that hint at **Yahweh’s grief** as well as Jeremiah’s.
- **Quote:** “The disputing of the shalom theology is a constant theme throughout the book of Jeremiah and a major issue of conflict between Jeremiah and other prophetic groups…. Deceit is what the prophets are prophesying in my name…. so there is at least a hint that the grief they express is Yahweh’s grief as well as Jeremiah’s…. ‘The religious establishment is bankrupt.’”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 357–379; on 14:13–18
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R5-09
- **Claim:** Goldingay reads 14:19–15:9 as a “more vehement rerun” of 14:2–18, with more weight on Yahweh’s threat; the section offers resources for reflecting on **corporate/generational responsibility** (ancestors’ waywardness, Manasseh) without excusing the present generation; neither Jeremiah nor the First Testament imagine serious turning followed by Yahweh still punishing for ancestors’ wrongdoing.
- **Quote:** “Once again, Jeremiah invites people to imagine making a protest to Yahweh…. This sequence constitutes ‘a more vehement rerun’ of 14:2–18…. The implication need not be that Yahweh will punish the second, third, and fourth generations irrespective of the nature of their own lives…. Neither Jeremiah nor other parts of the First Testament could imagine that Israel might engage in serious turning and Yahweh might still insist on punishing them for their ancestors’ wrongdoing.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 528–540; on 14:19–15:9
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R5-10
- **Claim:** On 15:1–4, Goldingay stresses that even if **Moses and Samuel** stood before Yahweh, he would not turn toward “this people”; exile-verbs and divorce-verbs underwrite the dismissal; four “kin groups” of death (sword, dogs, birds, animals) and calamity **on account of Manasseh** (with 2 Kgs 23:26; 24:3 parallel) make Judah a horror to the kingdoms of the earth.
- **Quote:** “If Moses and Samuel were to stand before me, my spirit would not be directed toward this people—send them off from before my face…. If Jeremiah is a prophet like Moses, his Moses-likeness takes an upside-down form…. I will make them into something horrifying to all earth’s kingdoms on account of Manasseh ben Hezekiah King of Judah…. While it is Jeremiah’s only mention of Manasseh, the comment fits the explanation for the fall of Jerusalem in 2 Kgs 23:26; 24:3.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 582–586; on 15:1–4
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R5-11
- **Claim:** Goldingay reads 15:5–9 as “the end of Jerusalem”: present generation cannot blame ancestors (*You yourself have deserted me*); Yahweh is “weary of relenting”; winnowing, making childless, widows “more numerous … than the sand of the seas” reverse ancestral promise; the mother of seven fades as her sun sets at midday—execution with “overtone of lament.”
- **Quote:** “No, the present generation cannot blame their parents…. I’ve got weary of relenting…. The circumlocution is followed by an image that is grievous in light of its usual context…. It implies a reversal of the promise to Israel’s ancestors…. Yes, vv. 5–9 are about ‘the end of Jerusalem.’ Yahweh speaks of the execution of judgment, but his words give vv. 7b–9 ‘an overtone of lament.’”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 588–598; on 15:5–9
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R5-12
- **Claim:** On 15:10–21, Goldingay reads Jeremiah’s **persecution protest** as more confrontational than 11:18–12:17, within a triangular dispute of YHWH, people/officials, and prophet; v. 10 addresses mother (Job 3 parallel): man of argument/contention with the entire country though he has neither lent nor borrowed; everyone “slighting” him.
- **Quote:** “This fourth exchange … starts with a protest by Jeremiah and ends with a robust response by Yahweh. It thus has a confrontational edge, like the exchange in 11:18–12:17, only more so…. It is ‘part of the dialogical or trialogical dispute which illustrates in highly dramatic fashion the triangular relationship between YHWH, his people and their officials, and YHWH’s prophet.’ … Rhetorically, Jeremiah addresses his mother, with sentiments that parallel those expressed at much greater length in Job 3.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 740–825; on 15:10–21 intro and v. 10
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R5-13
- **Claim:** Goldingay argues that the “you” of 15:11–14 is **Judah** (not Jeremiah), citing overlap with 17:3–4 and the unlikelihood of unannounced change of addressee; iron/bronze recall Jeremiah’s commission (1:18)—Judah cannot break him; Yahweh’s fire of anger (Deut 32:22) will burn against Judah’s stores and resources.
- **Quote:** “Although in vv. 11–12 you could be either Jeremiah or Judah, it must surely be Judah in vv. 13–14 … and it is unlikely that the identity of you changes without announcement there; therefore you in vv. 11–12 is also Judah…. Can iron break, especially when it is iron from the north? Can bronze break? … Judah is not to make the mistake of thinking that it can defeat Jeremiah or dispose of him. He will not break.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 703, 826–831; on 15:11–14
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R5-14
- **Claim:** In 15:15–18, Goldingay traces Jeremiah’s plea to his **commission** (acknowledge, mind, attend, redress; ate Yahweh’s words with joy; name proclaimed over him); he sat alone under Yahweh’s hand, filled with condemnation; long-temperedness is good for Judah but makes Yahweh “like a deceptive thing, water that can’t be trusted” because calamity is declared but never arrives.
- **Quote:** “You’ve actually become to me like a deceptive thing, water that cannot be trusted. A spring like Gihon flows all year…. But from time to time, a spring that people think is reliable stops flowing…. Such is Jeremiah’s image for Yahweh’s deceptive unreliability in relation to him…. Job said his friends were deceitful and unreliable that way (Job 6:14–21). Jeremiah says God is.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 833–839; on 15:15–18
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R5-15
- **Claim:** Goldingay reads Yahweh’s response (15:19–21) as non-guaranteed lament answer: Jeremiah must **turn** like Israel; “if you turn and I turn you” forbids taking acceptance for granted (relationship not contractual); he must utter “valuable” rather than “garbage,” become Yahweh’s mouth; people will turn to him but he must not turn to them; bronze-wall promise recycles 1:18–19 with added deliverance from faithless/terrifying.
- **Quote:** “Lament ‘does not provide a formula that guarantees God’s favorable response.’ … The implication is that Jeremiah is in the same position as Israel. He has turned away from Yahweh, and he needs to turn back…. There is an ‘if’ on Yahweh’s side as well as on theirs…. Then you will be my very mouth…. Those people will turn to you; but you—you will not turn to them…. Once again, Yahweh reverts to Jeremiah’s commission and recycles words from 1:18–19.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 840–846; on 15:19–21
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R5-16
- **Claim:** Goldingay’s pastoral-hermeneutical point on the confessions: most readers should **not** identify with Jeremiah’s protests unless they are figures like Bonhoeffer or King; the record confronts those who caused the trouble—“Let readers not be too quick to make these laments their own!”
- **Quote:** “Once more, Jeremiah gives an account of his agonizing not for his own sake, to let it all hang out, but to drive his hearers into looking at themselves. His protests are not ones that most readers should think to identify with, unless they are Dietrich Bonhoeffer or Martin Luther King Jr…. Let readers not be too quick to make these laments their own! That appropriating move may be a subtle way of avoiding the indictment the prophet speaks.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 846; on 15:20–21
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R5-17
- **Claim:** On 16:1–13, Goldingay treats Yahweh’s commission as **symbolic acts** (no marriage/children; no wake/mourning; no feasting): “flesh made word”; Jeremiah as passive stage-object/sign; “Hosea married a harlot to demonstrate the corruption of Israel’s relation to Yahweh, while [Jeremiah] married no one at all to demonstrate the end of Yahweh’s relation to Israel.”
- **Quote:** “Yahweh requires the prophet’s marriage status to serve his work as a prophet…. ‘Hosea married a harlot to demonstrate the corruption of Israel’s relation to Yahweh, while [Jeremiah] married no one at all to demonstrate the end of Yahweh’s relation to Israel.’ … A symbolic act is an exercise in rhetoric at least as much as a stage in the implementing of something…. ‘the flesh made word…. Jeremiah … has on this occasion become a (passive) stage object,’ turned into a sign.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 964–1054; on 16:1–4

### C-R5-18
- **Claim:** Goldingay emphasizes the **celibacy/no-children** command as countercultural and theologically shocking: marriage and children integral to creation and Abrahamic future; “in a move unparalleled in the Hebrew Bible, life is cut off before it begins”; children/parents die unlamented, unburied (manure, food for birds/animals) by sickness, sword, hunger—epidemic completing the unholy trinity.
- **Quote:** “Thus ‘in a move unparalleled in the Hebrew Bible, life is cut off before it begins’ while ‘those unlucky enough to be born already will die unmourned, and those who should by rights have been their mourners will not be comforted.’ … ‘These were not ordinary times’; Paul’s advice about marriage presupposes the same conviction (1 Cor 7).”

### C-R5-19
- **Claim:** Goldingay reads Yahweh’s withdrawal of **well-being, commitment, and compassion** (16:5) as a funeral for *šālôm*: gathering up compassion (*raḥămîm*, linked to womb) goes against Yahweh’s motherly nature; Jeremiah must embody future absence of mourning rites and of joy/groom/bride voice (16:9 // 7:34); exile will hurl them from the country with “no favor” (*ḥănînâ* hapax).
- **Quote:** “I have gathered up my well-being from this people…. Yahweh announces a funeral for well-being…. For Yahweh to gather up his compassion for Israel in order to bury it is to go against his motherly nature…. Here am I, stopping from this place … The voice of joy and the voice of rejoicing, the voice of groom and the voice of bride…. So I will hurl you from upon this country … in that I will show you no favor.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 1060–1069; on 16:5–13

### C-R5-20
- **Claim:** Against rhetorical expectation, Goldingay reads 16:14–15 as **fourth Deuteronomic aftermath** (return after exile): “therefore” is theo-logic, not logic; new foundational confession will be Yahweh who brought Israel up from the north and all countries, relativizing the Egypt exodus; after 587 Yahweh can talk mercifully after talking tough.
- **Quote:** “Deuteronomy has four ways of thinking about the catastrophe…. Against all rhetorical expectations, he now speaks in terms of the fourth…. The therefore following on the threat in v. 13 is in one sense illogical … But it does point to a deeper ‘theo-logic’…. now Jeremiah relativizes the exodus…. Generally speaking, in the decades up to 587 he talks tough, but after 587 he can be free to talk mercifully.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 1143–1169; on 16:14–15
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R5-21
- **Claim:** On 16:16–21, Goldingay argues juxtaposition reinterprets fishers/hunters and double recompense as **redress against the nations** (not Judah after 16:14–15), for defiling Yahweh’s country/domain with detestable corpses/offensive things; then nations from earth’s ends confess ancestral deceit and empty gods; Yahweh will make them acknowledge hand, strength, and name.
- **Quote:** “While the language in vv. 16–17 would make one think of Yahweh pursuing Judah … the recompense image suggests that Yahweh is rather talking about redress on the nations…. He will recompense them first, in a negative sense, before restoring Judah (vv. 14–15) and before getting the nations to acknowledge him (vv. 19–21)…. Jeremiah has urged Yahweh to pour out his wrath on the nations (10:25); vv. 16–18 are Yahweh’s response.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 1169–1199; on 16:16–21
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R5-22
- **Claim:** On 17:1–4, Goldingay reads Judah’s wrongdoing as **engraved with iron stylus/flint** on the mind’s tablet and altar horns—ingrained commitment to wrongdoing (// 13:23 leopard spots); mountain-dweller (Jerusalem) forfeits resources/shrines/domain; “for all time” (*ʿad-ʿôlām*) means foreseeable permanence until reason to change mind—not absolute eternity.
- **Quote:** “the problem is that it is Judah’s wrongdoing that is thus written or engraved…. a commitment to wrongdoing has become ingrained there…. The formulation is an alternative to asking whether a Sudanese can change his skin or a leopard its spots (13:23)…. Fortunately, the translation ‘forever’ … gives a misleading impression…. Commonly, it presupposes ‘until I have reason to change my mind,’ which safeguards against false confidence … but also against false despair.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 1369–1373; on 17:1–4
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R5-23
- **Claim:** Goldingay treats 17:5–11 as Proverbs-like Jeremianic teaching applied to Judah/king: **cursed** is the man who relies on flesh/humanity (steppe shrub in salt wilderness); **blessed** is the man who relies on Yahweh (tree by water, unafraid in heat/drought, still fruiting); mind is more devious than anything—Yahweh probes and recompenses paths/practices; partridge/ill-gotten wealth aphorism targets king (esp. Jehoiakim, 22:13).
- **Quote:** “The allegory’s implication is that disaster will follow if king and people think that their future lies in relying on a human being such as an Egyptian king…. The allegory’s positive implication is that king and people need to rely on Yahweh for their fate…. The mind is more devious than anything; it’s grave—who can know it? I, Yahweh, am probing the mind…. The aphorism becomes the means of commenting on Jeremiah’s expectations of a king … particularly the basis for Jeremiah’s critique of Jehoiakim…. ‘These innocent-looking affirmations hide the energy of prophecy.’”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 1375–1507; on 17:5–11
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R5-24
- **Claim:** On 17:12–27, Goldingay finds three ironies held by throne/sacredness/abandoning/shame: vv. 12–13a are **Judah’s** confessions (not Jeremiah’s temple enthusiasm); Jeremiah’s protest (14–18) ends with plea for double shattering of pursuers—Jeremiah has last word (silence of God matching absence announced to Israel); Sabbath command at People’s Gateway lays explicit **two destinies** (city lives forever vs. fire in gateways consuming citadels).
- **Quote:** “So the confessions in vv. 12–13a are the people’s confessions…. Whereas Yahweh has the last word in the exchanges in 11:18–12:17 and 14:13–15:21, Jeremiah has the last word here…. ‘The hostility he faces from human agents is matched by the silence of God…. The poet experiences the very absence that is the destiny of Israel.’ … While Jeremiah regularly implies an invitation to people to recognize that they have to choose between two destinies, here he explicitly lays alternatives before them…. ‘this passage, like much else in Jeremiah, stakes everything on the centrality of God.’”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 1680–1749; on 17:12–27
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R5-25
- **Claim:** Goldingay introduces Part 2d (18:1–20:18) via the curator formula “the message that came to Jeremiah from Yahweh”: two pot sequences with postscripts and protests; issue is **divine sovereignty vs. Judah’s decision-making**—first sequence future open (pot remade), second closed (pot smashed); before 587 challenge, after 587 explanation.
- **Quote:** “The issue the stories raise concerns divine sovereignty, and they thus raise questions about possible understandings of the relationship between Yahweh’s decision-making and Judah’s decision-making. In the first sequence, the future is still open (the pot can be remade); in the second, it is closed (the pot is smashed). Before 587, the compilation would confront the community with the necessity to take note of the challenge implied by the first sequence, before the closed future of the second set becomes a reality. After 587 it would summon the community to recognize the dynamic whereby things had worked out the way they had.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 1753–1755; Part 2d intro
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R5-26
- **Claim:** On 18:1–12, Goldingay stresses that the **anonymous potter** (not Jeremiah) performs the symbolic act on the double stones; clay “goes to ruin” (niphal, // 13:7)—potter reworks same clay, does not throw it away; “The good news for Judah is that Yahweh is not finished with it.”
- **Quote:** “A distinctive feature is that Jeremiah is not the one who performs the symbolic action itself…. The potter doesn’t cause the ruining; the shaping just doesn’t work out…. What the potter does is press the clay back into a ball and start again…. The potter does not throw away the clay he was working with and start again with a new ball of clay; he presses the clay back into a ball and reworks it. The respective theological implications of the two understandings would be radically different. The good news for Judah is that Yahweh is not finished with it.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 1896–1959; on 18:1–6
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R5-27
- **Claim:** Goldingay’s key theological claim on 18:7–10: Yahweh’s declarations about the future are not fixed by omniscient sovereignty; he speaks **“momentarily”**—threats are warnings meant to provoke response; if a nation turns from faithlessness, Yahweh **relents** of planned dire trouble; conversely he relents of promised good if it does what is dire; relationship is parental, not Western courtroom.
- **Quote:** “It’s possible for people to assume that God’s will is firmly fixed, that he is sovereign and all-knowing…. Such convictions can be a basis for both comfort and despair. Like other prophets, Jeremiah makes different assumptions. He knows Yahweh is more flexible than this theology implies…. His point is that there is nothing final about his statements concerning the future. He speaks momentarily, for a moment…. It was indeed a threat or warning: the point about it was to provoke a response that made its implementation unnecessary…. Yahweh’s relationship with people is more like that of parents with their children.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 1899, 1960–1968; on 18:7–10
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R5-28
- **Claim:** On 18:11–12, Goldingay links potter-image (*yôṣēr*) to Yahweh **shaping dire trouble** and formulating a plan: clay still unfired—people can turn and re-form the bad-news shaping; predicted response “Futile… after our own plans… determination of his dire mind” is defiance or despair put on their lips as challenge (// 2:25; 11:8); “Once it has become a pot, it will be too late (see 19:1–13).”
- **Quote:** “Yahweh is indeed shaping something, like a potter (*yôṣēr*)…. The good news is that it is specifically the bad-news shaping that can come to ruin in the potter’s hand, if the people turn…. Once it has become a pot, it will be too late (see 19:1–13). But at the moment the pot has not been fired. Thus in the meantime, God says, ‘Do not despair.’ … ‘The tragedy of Judah’s story is nowhere more poignantly set out than in the people’s response to these words’…. The story does imply that it’s still open to people to prove Yahweh and Jeremiah wrong.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 1969–1973; on 18:11–12
- **Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R5-29
- **Claim:** Goldingay reads 18:13–17 as postscript fleshing out Judah’s dire path: unnatural abandonment vs. Lebanon snow and foreign cold streams that do not pull up; people put Yahweh out of mind, burn to emptiness, leave age-long tracks for byways; Yahweh will scatter like east wind and show **back not face** on day of disaster.
- **Quote:** “It is totally ‘unnatural.’ … The snow thus lasts through the summer, doesn’t it? It doesn’t abandon its mountain….
